content:
Bloomberg yesterday reported that Apple is about to launch a brand new 'Apple Upgrade' lease contract to replace the existing iPhone Upgrade Program.

There seem to be two major differences between the two, one of which could be quite concerning...

The iPhone Upgrade Program works pretty simply. The purchase cost is spread over 24 months, and once that two-year period is up, the device is entirely yours, with no credit fees charged.

(You can also choose to upgrade to a new iPhone at the 12-month mark. A new two-year contract then begins, effectively trading in your old device to Apple for the amount you've already paid.)

Apple has not yet made any official announcement about the new plan, so the exact workings remain unconfirmed. However, Bloomberg indicated the new plan will cover most other Apple products, with Macs having a three-year term. That seems reasonable enough so far.

What's concerning, however, is that the report hints the new plan will operate much like an auto lease. With this type of contract, you're not paying off the full cost of the product over the lease term. Instead, your monthly payments only cover the depreciation during the lease period, plus any interest charges. When the term ends, you don't own the product—you've essentially been renting it the whole time.

Similarly, assuming it works like an auto lease, at the end of the term you'd have to return the product, or pay a 'residual' fee to cover the difference between the depreciation and the full price of the product.

Of course, this means your monthly payments would be lower than under the current plan. Some might see this as a good thing, since it could make Apple products more affordable for more consumers.

But here's what to watch out for: most people aren't going to be setting aside extra money each month so they can pay the residual at the end of the lease. The most common outcome with auto leases is that the lessee returns the car at the end and signs a new lease on a new car. They're stuck in a perpetual cycle, never truly owning the product.

If the new Apple Upgrade plan works the same way, that's exactly what would happen. Consumers would no longer have the option of keeping their current phone for several years—they'd essentially be forced to upgrade their iPhone every two years, or their Mac every three. Even without any interest charges, the lifetime cost of ownership would still rise significantly.

Additionally, if the report is accurate and AppleCare+ isn't included, should your device be lost, stolen, or damaged beyond repair during the lease term, you'd be in a bind: not only would you continue making monthly payments on a device you no longer have, you'd also have to pay the residual at the end of the lease.

I can understand Apple wanting to streamline things with a single upgrade plan and phase out the current option. But I think the better move for consumers would be to offer a choice of different plans, so people can take advantage of the credit arrangement while also deciding for themselves how often to upgrade.

What are your thoughts on this? Feel free to share your opinions in the comments section.
